标题: Lowe’s Says ‘Semantic’ Data is Boosting Its AI Agents
内容:
Microsoft, Databricks, SAP and other AI software providers are fighting over control and access to enterprise data known as the semantic layer,
as we reported last week
.
Semantic layers are essentially a data management tool that companies use to standardize definitions for their business metrics, such as revenue and customers, and are now enabling AI to work more accurately and efficiently inside enterprises.
Retailer Lowe’s, for instance, recently began using its semantic layer and another tool that defines how different types of corporate data are connected to each other—knowledge graphs—to improve how its AI agents help customers with orders or helping store managers coordinate the day-to-day work that employees do in stores, said Chandhu Nair, a senior vice president.
Lowe’s runs an AI-powered shopping assistant for customers and an AI sales coach for its employees, both of which it developed with OpenAI over the past couple of years. Lowe’s also developed a customized agent that helps its finance teams verify that invoices are processed accurately, which is important because of the volume of invoices it handles as the fifth-largest importer in the U.S., Nair said.
Tapping the semantic data and knowledge graphs became possible due to open-source tools the company used to develop its internal AI platform, which it uses for everything from developing agents to tracking employees’ token consumption. Advanced reasoning models and agent-development tools from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, which are Lowe's main AI providers, also improved the capabilities of the platform, said Nair.
If a Lowe’s AI agent detects that a customer’s order is delayed, he said, it can work with other systems that track order information, inventory levels and data about product availability from suppliers to identify a more precise cause of the delay and suggest ways to fix the problem, Nair said. (If that sounds similar, it’s because a sensor component firm
in this story last week uses AI for a similar purpose involving its supply chain
.)
Lowe‘s also uses multiple agents to coordinate and maintain product inventory levels during times of heavy demand, such as promotions, which isn’t possible without the contextual data it is now able to use, said Nair.
“If the merchandising team, the promotions team, and the inventory team have the same context about the decisions they make, they can make much more effective decisions,” he said. “That is a critical part of how we run our business today, and that context layer is a differentiating factor.”
Another potential benefit of contextual data is that it could make agents cheaper to run, as they don’t have to “think” as much to make decisions, though Nair said it’s too early to tell if Lowe’s AI costs are dropping after giving its agents access to this kind of data.
But there’s no doubt that giving AI better data to work with will be necessary to convince large companies to expand AI budgets at a time when many customers,
including sophisticated ones like Uber
, are still struggling to measure a return on their AI investments.
Salesforce’s Subscription Revenue Split and What it Could Mean
Salesforce did a curious thing in its first earnings report for its fiscal 2027, splitting its subscription revenue products into two buckets. One of them contains older applications like Slack, customer management and marketing automation while the other includes newer products like Data 360 (formerly known as Data Cloud) and Headless 360, a recently unveiled set of tools that lets customers use AI agents from companies like Anthropic to access their Salesforce data.
The two new buckets show Salesforce is trying to transition from selling traditional business applications to products that customers can use to develop and use agents that, for example, process invoices and resolve customer service inquiries. Revenue for Salesforce’s traditional applications grew around 9% in its April quarter compared to last year, while its AI products grew around 25% during that period. (The newer AI products haven’t boosted its overall sales growth much, however. Read more
here
.)
Vernon Keenan, a software industry analyst who covers Salesforce, sees the move as a way to highlight the growth of its AI products. “By isolating seat-based revenue into a new bucket, Salesforce is making a slight nod to the SaaSpocalypse by making sure growth in agentic consumption won’t get diluted by the expected decrease in the number of seats sold over time,” he said.

标题: The AI Boom’s Pricey Middle
内容:
Baseten’s talks to raise fresh funding at an $11 billion valuation are the
latest sign
that investors are betting the messy work of helping developers run AI models can become one of the next big businesses in AI.
That boom has lifted a group of companies including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Together AI and Modal. These startups give customers access to GPU capacity and offer software that makes AI models easier to customize and deploy, and have seen revenue surge recently. The question now is how durable that revenue will be as competition heats up and customers learn to do more of the work themselves.
Inference providers sit between developers, model makers and the cloud providers that supply much of the underlying computing power, which has been a valuable position as companies rush to put models into production. But competition can push prices and margins lower, making it more important for these companies to prove they offer something customers cannot easily get elsewhere. Deep Research analyzed how inference providers can keep supporting fast growth and high valuations, and what could still cause them to get squeezed out of the equation.
Deep Research Prompt
Evaluate the role and prospects of inference providers like Baseten, Fireworks, Together and Modal in the broader AI infrastructure ecosystem. Map out the biggest known customers of inference provider startups. Identify risks and opportunities for the business models of inference providers.
Deep Research Response
The artificial intelligence inference sector has transformed from a niche category with questionable unit economics into one of the most explosive segments of the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Inference providers—notably Baseten, Fireworks AI, Together AI, and Modal—fill a critical gap: they rent out Nvidia servers to application developers and provide the software scaffolding needed to easily customize and run open-source models like Meta’s Llama, Mistral’s Mixtral, and Alibaba’s Qwen.
While the core of their business resembles standard cloud reselling, these startups have differentiated themselves by allowing developers to bypass the high costs and complexity of managing AI infrastructure directly. However, despite their massive revenue growth, inference providers face structural threats regarding their gross margins and the looming shadow of mega-cap cloud providers.
The Role and Current Prospects
The prospect for inference providers has shifted dramatically over the past year. In early 2024, skeptics warned that inference startups risked getting steamrolled by traditional cloud providers. But by early 2026, the explosion of applications built on open-source AI models catapulted these companies to staggering valuations.
1,2
To understand their scale as of May 2026:
Together AI
reached approximately $1 billion in annualized revenue by March 2026, raising funds at an $8.5 billion post-money valuation.
Fireworks AI
passed $800 million in annualized revenue in May 2026 (more than double its October 2025 pace) and entered talks to triple its valuation to $15 billion.
Baseten
reached $600 million in annualized revenue by the end of Q1 2026—a 20-fold increase year-over-year—and has been in talks to raise $1 billion at an $11 billion valuation.
Modal
saw its annualized revenue balloon to more than $300 million by the spring of 2026, jumping five times from the previous fall, and recently raised at a $4.65 billion valuation.
View full chart: Inference Engine
As the chart illustrates, the velocity of capital flowing into these platforms reflects an immense developer appetite for open-source model execution.
The Customer Map
The customer base for inference providers tends to segment based on the specific optimizations each provider offers:
Fireworks AI
has ridden the coattails of some of the fastest-growing AI application startups. It relies heavily on high-volume developers, with its revenue aided significantly by mega-customers like AI coding assistant
Cursor
and AI search engine
Perplexity
.
3,4
Modal
specifically targets startup developers who prioritize “developer experience” and fast iteration, offering unique environments to quickly get models up and running.
4,5
Baseten
leans more heavily toward enterprise customers, focusing heavily on allowing larger organizations to securely use their own proprietary data to fine-tune open-source models.
4,5
The Business Model: Risks and the Margin Squeeze
While their top-line growth is staggering, the fundamental business model of an inference provider comes with financial risks:
1. The Reseller Margin Squeeze:
Unlike traditional cloud providers that own their hardware, inference startups generally rent GPUs from larger providers (like CoreWeave or AWS) and then sublease them to developers. This deeply depresses gross profit margins. For instance, in early 2024, Modal’s gross margin was roughly 10%, while Fireworks hovered around 50%—a far cry from the 70%-plus margins typical of traditional SaaS businesses.
4
The scarcity of AI chips, driven by mega-buyers like Anthropic and OpenAI, has repeatedly pushed up spot prices, further squeezing the middleman.
2
2. Utilization Pressures and “Noisy Neighbors”:
To ensure they can handle sudden spikes in their customers’ application traffic, inference providers must keep up to half of their rented servers unused at any given time. Conversely, because many developers share the same API (to allow providers to “batch” queries and save money), a spike from one customer can slow down inference speeds for others—a problem known as “noisy neighbors.”
4,6
3. Price Wars and Big Tech Encroachment:
Because the underlying open-source models (like Llama or Mixtral) are identical across platforms, differentiation is difficult. This has led to aggressive price wars. For example, when Mistral released Mixtral in December 2023, inference startups drove prices down from $2 per million tokens to 27 cents in just days, with some subsidizing the cost below profitability using their venture funding.
6
Furthermore, Nvidia itself is becoming a direct competitor. In March 2026, Nvidia acquired inference provider Lepton AI and used it to launch a GPU cloud marketplace that effectively competes with startups like Fireworks.
3
Opportunities and Strategic Pivots
To survive the margin squeeze, inference providers are pivoting away from pure compute resale and moving up the software stack:
1. Premium Enterprise Services:
Inference startups are looking to offer products they can charge a premium for. Baseten, for example, acquired the startup Parsed in December 2025 to help enterprise customers easily fine-tune open-source models with their proprietary data. Modal’s growth is heavily tied to a “sandbox” product that allows developers to safely run AI agents and execute code without risking their core codebase.
1,2
2. The DeepSeek Tailwinds:
The release of highly capable, ultra-cheap Chinese models like DeepSeek V3 in early 2025 presented a massive opportunity. Because U.S. enterprises refuse to send their proprietary data to Chinese servers due to security risks, developers flocked to third-party providers like Together AI to run DeepSeek locally and securely. Together AI reworked its software to spread the massive DeepSeek model across dozens of Nvidia chips, serving as a vital bridge between foreign open-source innovation and domestic data security.
7
3. Consolidation and M&A:
Finally, the inference layer is ripe for consolidation. The underlying work these startups do on chip optimization—getting Nvidia GPUs to run faster and communicate more efficiently—makes them highly attractive acquisition targets. Our reporting indicates that major cloud providers like CoreWeave and model makers are closely monitoring these startups to internalize their efficiency gains.
3,8
Ultimately, while the current revenue multiples are astronomical, the long-term survival of Baseten, Fireworks, Together, and Modal relies on their ability to transition from being simple GPU tollbooths to becoming indispensable, high-margin software infrastructure platforms.

标题: The AI Data Center Boom Ignites a Tear in Lithium Shares
内容:
Investors fled the stock of
lithium mining companies in 2022 and 2023, when the metal’s price plunged about 90% and mines shut down globally. Now they have piled back into the category. The reason: a boom in lithium-ion batteries used to power AI data centers and the electricity grid, and the possibility that high gasoline prices will trigger a jump in electric vehicle sales.
Over the last year, shares of South Carolina–based Albemarle, the world’s largest lithium miner, have soared 202%; Chilean lithium miner SQM’s shares have gone up 156%; and Australian miner PLS Group’s, a whopping 376%.
Investors are reacting because the miners are suddenly profitable again, with lithium now selling for roughly $25 a kilogram, three times the price in November.
That ebullience, however, masks a sustained underlying fear that lithium’s bad days may not be over. A significant reason for the 2022–23 lithium crash was a flood of Chinese lithium onto the global market, and some analysts predict that miners from China and other countries will once again deluge the market and send lithium prices back down.
For now, though, lithium companies have begun to reopen closed mines and are spending to develop new ones.
On Monday, Australian miner Mineral Resources said it and Chinese miner Ganfeng Lithium would spend $352 million to develop a new section of Mount Marion, an existing lithium mine in Western Australia. Mineral Resources made the announcement a week after saying it would reopen Bald Hill, a lithium mine in Western Australia that it shut down 18 months ago.
Last week, Core Lithium said it would reopen the Finniss lithium mine in Australia’s Northern Territory two years after closing the operation.
“The market’s superexcited about lithium because this time last year, it was bleak. It was terrible. Everyone wanted to slit their wrists,” said Howard Klein, founder of RK Equity, a firm that researches battery metals.
Lithium’s rebound reflects the reality that regardless of laggard EV demand in the U.S., the metal is key in the batteries of virtually every major electronic device—smartphones, drones, laptops, humanoid robots, satellites, you name it. Lithium-ion batteries help power AI data centers and homes. Lithium is attractive for such uses because it’s the lightest metal on the periodic table and holds an exceptional amount of energy for its weight.
The recovery in the lithium market is also part of a new boom across metals and fuels as investors reawaken to the enduring and powerful role of traditional industrial commodities in the global economy.
Oil is the most prominent example: Until the Iran war, investors seemed to almost forget how much cash major oil companies could generate. Alongside oil, the prices of most major battery metals have soared for various reasons, mostly involving local politics in places where the mining takes place, like Zimbabwe and Indonesia. Nickel prices are up about 25% over the last year, and cobalt is up about 67%.
President Donald Trump’s metals nationalism has contributed to the general euphoria around the sector. In October, for instance, the Trump administration approved a
$2.2 billion government loan
to Nevada-based Lithium Americas. As part of the deal, the U.S. received a 5% stake in the company and a separate 5% stake in Thacker Pass, Lithium Americas’ giant lithium mine. At the time, the company’s shares rose 23% on the news. While its share price has since come down, it is still up 80% over the last 12 months.
Trump is generally hostile toward EVs but backed the loan because the military uses vast numbers of lithium ion batteries.
The last peak of lithium prices came in November 2022, when they rose to around $80/kg. The spike reflected a battery mania as industry veterans had forecast massive EV demand and a gigantic shortfall of lithium over the 2020s.
But that shortfall did not materialize, and lithium prices began to decline steeply, reaching around $8/kg in early 2024. The main cause was an unexpected surge in the supply of lithium obtained from lepidolite, a rock in China’s Jiangxi province. Western lithium analysts had ridiculed the idea of lepidolite as a viable contender because the average concentration of lithium in it is extremely low and it is expensive to mine.
But Chinese companies figured out that they could profitably sell numerous byproducts from the mining, said Chris Berry, president of House Mountain Partners, a metals research firm.
Now some analysts are forecasting a surge of supply from Jiangxi. In a
report last week
, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, a battery metals research firm, predicted that Jiangxi’s lepidolite would feed a lithium surplus starting next year and lasting at least until 2030. One of the main factors in its forecast is resumed production at a large Jiangxi lepidolite mine owned by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd., the world’s biggest battery producer, said Cameron Perks, Benchmark's product director for lithium.
“You know what happens when the Chinese get onto a bandwagon and they’re all like, ‘I’ve got to produce, I’ve got to produce, I’ve got to produce.’ That’s what’s happening,” said Matt Fernley, a partner at RK Equity.

标题: Apple to Renew Push for AI That Runs on Devices, Instead of the Cloud
内容:
At Apple’s annual developer conference next month, the star of the show will be a series of long-delayed artificial intelligence upgrades to the iPhone. But the company is also expected to emphasize what could be an underrated asset in its efforts to catch up in AI: Its ability to run AI models on the billions of
Apple
devices in circulation.
People familiar with the company’s plans for its Worldwide Developers Conference say that Apple is likely to showcase how the company’s 15 years of experience of designing custom silicon chips for iPhones, Watches and Macs will give it an advantage when running AI models locally on those devices. Typically, AI models are run in expensive data centers filled with powerful AI chips.
Many AI queries from Apple’s devices will still have to be processed in the cloud because of their complexity and need for access to troves of online information. For example, as part of an Apple
agreement
with Google, some user queries to a new version of Siri will run in Google Cloud on a licensed version of the search giant’s Gemini model. Apple recently approved the use of a privacy technology from Nvidia in that setting, suggesting it will use Nvidia AI chips for at least some of its computing needs in Google Cloud, according to people familiar with the matter.
But running models locally could reduce the risk of exposing consumers’ data and prevent advertising companies from monetizing their personal information. It could save business customers money by reducing their consumption of “tokens”—the units of text that cloud AI models base their pricing on. And for Apple, pushing more AI chores onto devices could allow it to continue to avoid the eye-watering investments its tech peers have made in data centers.
As part of its Google agreement, Apple is using a version of Google’s large Gemini model to train a smaller version of the model that can run locally on Apple devices, a process known as distillation, said people familiar with the effort. Apple is also on the lookout to acquire smaller companies that can assist in the effort of shrinking down AI models to run on its devices, people familiar with the company said. One such company it has considered acquiring is Liquid AI, a Cambridge, Mass.-based startup specializing in running AI locally on devices, said people familiar with Apple’s strategy.
Apple first began touting the privacy benefits of running models on devices in 2024, when it introduced Apple Intelligence, a collection of new AI features it announced at the time. Since then, it has largely been quiet on the topic, after an embarrassing series of stumbles, including a tepid response to its new AI features and a delay with the launch of the new Siri.
At the same time, Apple has largely sat on the sidelines as the biggest companies in tech have poured fortunes into building AI computing capacity in the cloud. Last year, Meta Platforms, for example, spent $72 billion on capital expenditures—mostly stemming from data centers—while Microsoft spent $88 billion. Apple, meanwhile, spent only $12.72 billion on capital expenditures during that period.
At times, the company’s hesitation to pour more money into AI has prompted criticism from investors and pundits who believe the company could risk being left behind in a future where AI is a key ingredient in personal devices. As the tech industry’s AI investments have swelled to mammoth proportions—Microsoft, for one, is projecting $190 billion in capital expenditures this year—some technologists have started to worry about overspending on AI computing capacity and look more favorably at Apple’s relatively conservative bets in the category.
“I think the data center boom is a mistake,” said David Stout, chief executive of Austin-based AI startup webAI. “Intelligence is getting smaller. Data centers won’t disappear, but the majority of work will happen at the edge. Apple made the bet correctly there.”
Stout is among a growing cohort of AI developers who are making bets on new businesses based on Apple hardware. WebAI develops specialized AI applications for enterprises that run locally on Apple chips. For example, webAI builds tools for aviation customers with an AI trained on a massive manual describing the intricacies of a Boeing Dreamliner engine to assist in engine maintenance.
The models can run on an iPad or Mac, without the need for an internet connection. Apple’s computers have also taken off among techies who use them to run OpenClaw, an open-source tool for creating AI agents that can autonomously run a computer.
Technology analyst Richard Kramer of Arete Research said in a recent note to investors that he estimates Apple has $50 billion worth of compute capacity in on-device chips “funded by users.”
Mark Suman, a former Apple senior engineering project manager who worked on internal AI systems before leaving in 2024, said that the billions of Apple devices around the world collectively amount to a powerful source of AI computing capacity.
“Apple could deploy the largest edge-compute AI that anybody has in the world,” said Suman, who is now co-founder of Maple, a startup offering customers an encrypted system for accessing AI models in the cloud. “It’s really a matter of time before they leverage that.”
Apple still can’t rely entirely on on-device models for its AI strategy. Google’s full Gemini model has trillions of parameters—a rough measure of the complexity of an AI model. The full model requires so much computing horsepower that Apple has struggled to get it to work on its own internal server infrastructure, called Private Cloud Compute, which runs on the same Apple chips in Mac computers, said people familiar with the situation.
Apple will likely have to take advantage of Google’s cloud infrastructure to run parts of the new Siri, former Apple engineers said. Still, Apple is looking for ways to run AI services in the cloud while still offering improved privacy protections. Its decision in recent weeks to approve the use of Nvidia’s confidential compute system to handle some of the processing of the bigger Gemini-based model inside Google Cloud is one such effort, people familiar with the partnership said.
Confidential compute is a security feature inside Nvidia graphics processing units that encrypts data and AI models as they are being processed. When enabled, it slightly slows down the processing of AI queries in the cloud, but it could help Apple keep its promises about protecting users’ privacy.
The plan would also represent a reversal from Apple’s original announcement of Apple Intelligence, in which the company said that Apple hardware inside its  Private Cloud Compute system would process all AI queries that weren’t processed locally on users’ devices. Despite that, Apple is likely to continue to use the Private Cloud Compute brand, said people familiar with the partnership.
